catalog_locator: Bauza 1996 p.505, section 'Prosodic Features'; also p.502 'Proposal for Change'. Peace Corps 1968 p.3 = p.21.
catalog_quote: Stress in Ibanag is phonemic. A change in stress signals a change in meaning. Examples: agal ("call"); agál ("liver); pitu ("whistle"); pitú ("seven"); anâ ("son, daughter"); anà ("offspring, children"). Intonation and rhythm depend upon the unstressed and stressed syllables of speech. In an utterance, important words are stressed with one primary stress occurring in the utterance. [p.505] ... we could adopt the "maragsa" symbol [ ^] for words stressed on the last syllable, and the "malumi" symbol [ `] for words stressed on the second to the last syllable. Examples: allô ("pity"); makimallò ("to pray, to ask for pity"); anâ ("child"); anà ("children, offspring"). Note in this last example that the change in stress also signals a change in meaning from singular to plural. [p.502] || Peace Corps 1968 p.3: Stress. Stress is phonemic. Thus the position of the stress distinguishes /batu/ 'cue ball' from /batú/ 'stone.' Stressed vowels are usually longer than unstressed vowels and also higher in pitch. However, if two or more syllables follow a stress, the syllable immediately following the stress has a higher pitch than the stressed syllable. ... 2. Primary stress, which most frequently occurs on the final syllable, is not marked in that position. When it occurs elsewhere, it is written with an acute accent.
world_status: statement found in an open source

Examples: agal ("call"); agál ("liver); pitu ("whistle"); pitú ("seven"); anâ ("son, daughter"); anà ("offspring, children"). new_statements.citation: Bauza, Humberto G. 1996. A Proposal to Modify Ibanag Orthography. Philippiniana Sacra 31(93): 501-507.
new_statements.locator: p.505, section 'Prosodic Features' (also p.502 'Proposal for Change')
new_statements.second_reader_evidence: Quote check: rendered p.505 (PDF page 5) of to an image and read it. Under the heading 'Prosodic Features' the text reads exactly: 'Stress in Ibanag is phonemic. A change in stress signals a change in meaning. Examples: agal ("call"); agál ("liver); pitu ("whistle"); pitú ("seven"); anâ ("son, daughter"); anà ("offspring, children"). Intonation and rhythm depend upon the unstressed and stressed syllables of speech. In an utterance, important words are stressed with one primary stress occurring in the utterance.' -- verbatim as reported (the PDF's OmniPage text garbles anâ/anà as 'anti'/'and', but the page scan matches the report). p.502 'Proposal for Change' also confirmed on the image: mar…
new_statements.rule_in_words: Word stress is lexically contrastive between the penultimate and the final syllable (agal vs agál, pitu vs pitú, bátu 'stone'.. etc.); it is not fixed by position. Corroborated first-hand by Peace Corps/Pascasio 1968 p.3 ('Stress is phonemic.. /batu/ cue ball vs /batú/ stone'; primary stress 'most frequently occurs on the final syllable'; stressed vowels longer and higher-pitched), by Brandes & Scheerer 1927 p.10 (ultima stress marked with acute, otherwise 'the weight of the voice falls, thru duration, on the penult'), and by Ibarbia 1969 p.x (one prominent syllable per word, 'generally the penultimate or the final'). Cuevas 1854 and Bauza 1996 add that accent shift alone can mark plural (Abbíng > Ábbing; anâ > anà).
new_statements.secondary_stress: None of the sources describes secondary stress; Peace Corps 1968 notes a post-tonic syllable may carry higher pitch than the stressed syllable when two or more syllables follow the stress.
new_statements.exceptions: Sources disagree on which position is the unmarked/more frequent one: Brandes & Scheerer 1927 treat penult (realised as vowel duration) as the default and mark only ultima stress; Peace Corps 1968 says primary stress most frequently falls on the final syllable and marks only non-final stress; Ibarbia 1969 says stress 'shifts' in context and 'does not seem to be as important in Ibanag as it is in English'. Accent shift to the first syllable forms plurals of some kin terms (Cuevas 1854 num.53, 56; Bauza 1996 p.502) and emphatic superlatives (Cuevas num.119).
new_statements.domain_note: Statements concern the word in citation form (dictionary headwords, minimal pairs); Bauza and Ibarbia separately note one primary stress per utterance/phrase in connected speech. Variety: Tuguegarao (Central) Ibanag for Peace Corps 1968 and Bauza 1996; Brandes & Scheerer's speaker also Tuguegarao.
new_statements.identity_note: All quoted sources describe Ibanag proper (iban1267), mostly the Tuguegarao (Central/'standard') variety: Peace Corps 1968 and Bauza 1996 are based on Tuguegarao speech (speaker H. G. Bauza), Brandes & Scheerer 1927's informant likewise Tuguegarao; Verstraelen's text is from Pamplona (Northern Ibanag). No separate glottocodes for these dialects.

new_statements.quote: Stress. Stress is phonemic. Thus the position of the stress distinguishes /batu/ 'cue ball' from /batú/ 'stone.' Stressed vowels are usually longer than unstressed vowels and also higher in pitch. However, if two or more syllables follow a stress, the syllable immediately following the stress has a higher pitch than the stressed syllable. [...] 2. Primary stress, which most frequently occurs on the final syllable, is not marked in that position. When it occurs elsewhere, it is written with an acute accent (´). Thus /batú/ 'stone' is written batu, while /bátu/ 'cue ball' is written bátu.

Orthography item 2 reads verbatim: 'Primary stress, which most frequently occurs on the final syllable, is not marked in that position. When it occurs elsewhere, it is written with an acute accent (´). Thus /batú/ 'stone' is written batu, w…
new_statements.relation_note: Agrees with the existing statement (Bauza 1996: 'Stress in Ibanag is phonemic') that stress is contrastive and lexically specified, and adds the statistical tendency toward final stress, the phonetic correlates (length, pitch, post-stress high pitch) and a minimal pair. The analysis is by Emy M. Pascasio on the speech of Humberto G. Bauza of Tuguegarao, the same person who wrote the 1996 orthography proposal already in the catalog, so the two statements rest on one speaker/variety.
new_statements.rule_in_words: Word stress is contrastive (minimal pair batú 'stone' vs bátu 'cue ball'); it most often falls on the final syllable but can fall elsewhere, so it must be marked lexically. Phonetic correlates: the stressed vowel is longer and higher in pitch, except that when two or more syllables follow the stress the syllable right after it is higher in pitch than the stressed one.
new_statements.secondary_stress: Only 'primary stress' is mentioned; no statement on secondary stress. Peace Corps p.17 (bundle p.35) adds that in the distributive-numeral list 'by exception, every primary stress is marked with an acute accent'.
new_statements.exceptions: Stress is said to fall 'most frequently' on the final syllable; non-final stress is the exception and is marked with an acute in the booklet's orthography.
new_statements.identity_note: Peace Corps 1968 is explicitly based on the speech of Humberto G. Bauza, a mother-tongue speaker of Ibanag as spoken at Tuguegarao, Cagayan (analysis by Emy M. Pascasio, Ateneo Language Center); the catalog's existing Bauza 1996 statement comes from the same speaker. The Zorc sheets are dated 74.11.21 and 75.9.4 (Glottolog lists them as 1972) and are comparative lexicostatistics, not a description of a specific variety.

sources.citation: Fausto de Cuevas, José María. 1854 [1826]. Arte nuevo de la lengua Ybanag. 2a ed. Manila. 432 pp. (ONB Austrian Books Online Z156915903, scanned text via IIIF)
sources.note: Libro I cap. I-II (letters, vowels, diphthongs, geminates) has no general accent rule; words carry acute accents on penult or final (Babáy, Baláy, Danúm vs Bábbay, Bábbal); num.53 and 56: certain kin nouns form the plural 'con solo mudarles el acento a la primera sílaba' (Abbíng > Ábbing; Babáy > Bábbay); num.119: superlatives by accent shift with lengthening. Implies contrastive, morphologically exploitable accent.
